title: Recheck fairly
goal: Learn to make the computer pick three jars at random, by chance. That is fair: every jar has the same chance. Round 2 is where Julia differs most from R.
story: Itchy, the lab head, wants a slow look at three of Eddie's five open jars, one afternoon each. The jars are made up. You will let the computer pick the three by luck.
story_more: A recheck is a slow, leaf-by-leaf look at a jar, because a quick two-minute look can miss springtails hiding in the leaves. Itchy can only recheck 3 jars, one each afternoon. Five jars are open: Q-071, Q-072, Q-074, Q-077 and Q-078. Eddie, who keeps the records, put them in a table called open_jars. It has one column, jar_id. Toto, the eager one in the lab: "Let the computer pick 3 at random, so nobody chooses favourites." Two jars are left out because there are only three afternoons. A random pick keeps it fair: every jar has the same chance, 3 in 5. The data are made up for practice.

glossary.means: one instruction for Julia, written in code.
to press the Run button, so Julia does what your line says.
facts set out in a grid: one thing on each row, one kind of detail in each column.
one kind of detail running down a table, such as jar_id.
several things one after another, in order, such as a column of jar ids.
a word that does a job on whatever you put inside its round brackets ( ).
something you put inside a function's round brackets ( ) for it to work on.
an input with its own name, written name=value after a semicolon, such as replace=false.
what an input is set to, such as false in replace=false.
the mark ; that goes before a named input.
the mark . that joins a table name and a column name, as in practice_jars.jar_id.
the mark , that keeps two inputs apart.
the ___ in a line. Type your answer in its place.
all the whole numbers from one number to another, written like 1:6.
a number with no decimal part, such as 3.
the marks " " around text.
the only two answers to a yes-or-no question. Julia writes them in small letters.
decided by luck, not by anyone's choice.
every jar has the same chance to be picked.
the function that picks things at random, like drawing from a bag.
a named input of sample. With false, a picked one is not put back, so it cannot be picked twice.
the low line _ that joins words in a name, as in jar_id.
big letters such as A and B. Julia treats first and First as different words.
the button under the editor that puts the starting line back.

own_work.say: On a laptop, install StatsBase once (first line), then load it each time. A seed is a starting number: after using Random, Random.seed!(42) repeats the same picks, which are not the picks R's set.seed(42) gives. mydata is a placeholder.
own_work.code:
# Install once, the first time only:
using Pkg; Pkg.add("StatsBase")
# Each time you start Julia:
using StatsBase, Random
Random.seed!(42)
sample(mydata.id, 3; replace=false)

can_do: Give a function two inputs, like first(list, 3).
Pick things at random with sample and replace=false.
Check a random pick when no one answer is right.
close.common_mistake: Leaving out replace=false, so sample can pick the same jar twice. Julia's sample puts each pick back unless you stop it.
